narrativeProgression.description: Plants dominate the landscape and are integral to life on Earth.
Plants influence climate, provide nutrition and medicinal compounds, and offer numerous bioproducts.
Plants evolved about 475 million years ago from green algae and currently encompass over 300,000 species, most of which are photoautotrophs.

activities.description: Presentation of text and diagram illustrating the alternation of generations in plants

narrativeProgression.description: Land plants alternate between multicellular haploid (gametophyte) and diploid (sporophyte) generations.
Spores are diploid and develop into the gametophyte which produces haploid gametes. The relationship between sporophyte and gametophyte varies among plant groups.
As plants evolved, the gametophyte generation has become reduced, sometimes to a microscopic level. Simple algae show a more prominent gametophyte generation.

narrativeProgression.description: Land plants are classified into two major groups: nonvascular and vascular plants, depending on the presence or absence of vascular tissue.
Nonvascular plants include bryophytes, liverworts, mosses, and hornworts.
Vascular plants include seedless and seed plants.
Vascular tissue comprises xylem for water transport and phloem for nutrient transport.
Nonvascular plants have specialized cells for water and nutrient transport.

activities.description: Presentation of text and images describing characteristics and examples of bryophytes

narrativeProgression.description: Bryophytes are green, seedless plants, considered as lower level land plants. Examples include mosses, liverworts, and hornworts.
The gametophyte stage is more prominent in bryophytes, requiring water for sperm cells to reach egg cells. As a result, bryophytes are commonly found near water sources like lakes and swamps.

Liverworts resemble the lobes of a liver, hence the name. Hornworts have a short, blue-green gametophyte emerging from the sporophyte. Ferns and whisk ferns are characterized by larger leaves and branching roots.

activities.description: Presentation of text and images illustrating characteristics and examples of gymnosperms

narrativeProgression.description: Gymnosperms were the first plants to colonize land and resemble modern-day plants.
Gymnosperms have 'naked seeds' and are a diverse group descended from a common ancestor. They have separate male and female gametes, pollinated by wind and insects through cones.
Examples include conifers (pine trees), cycads (pollinated by beetles), and the ginkgo tree (fan-shaped leaves). Gymnosperms lack ovaries but possess ovules (containing eggs) in female cones.

activities.description: Presentation of text and images explaining the characteristics and diversity of angiosperms

narrativeProgression.description: Angiosperms are the flowering plants, contributing to a beautiful landscape, pollinated by birds, bees, bats, and other animals.
Angiosperms are divided into two main classes: monocots (e.g., lily, grassy plants) and dicots (woody branches).

Most flowering plants have a reduced gametophyte stage. Gametes are confined to flowers, which carry both male and female organs. The diagram showcases the life cycle of a flowering plant, including pollen grains and the embryo sac.

activities.description: Presentation of text and diagram explaining double fertilization in flowering plants

narrativeProgression.description: Flowering plants undergo double fertilization, a unique process to angiosperms.
A haploid sperm combines with a haploid egg to form a zygote.
Another sperm fuses with two polar nuclei to form endosperm, providing nutrition to the zygote.

activities.description: Presentation of a chart comparing structural characteristics of monocots and dicots, along with illustrative images

narrativeProgression.description: Monocots have one small cotyledon (e.g., corn seeds). Bean seeds, which can split into two parts, are dicots.
Monocots have parallel leaf veins (e.g., tulips, corn, grass). Dicots have branched or 'woody branched' leaves.
Another difference is the number of flower parts. Monocots typically have flower parts in multiples of three, while dicots have them in multiples of four or five.
